## Token labeling: one shared head, many decisions {#ts-ner .ts-slide}

<p class="ts-lead">Named-entity recognition identifies <strong>entity boundaries and types</strong>.</p>
<table class="ts-token-table"><thead><tr><th>Word</th><th>Lina</th><th>studies</th><th>at</th><th>New</th><th>York</th><th>University</th><th>.</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th>Gold BIO tag</th><td class="ts-person">B-PER</td><td>O</td><td>O</td><td class="ts-org">B-ORG</td><td class="ts-org">I-ORG</td><td class="ts-org">I-ORG</td><td>O</td></tr><tr><th>Contextual state</th><td>h₀</td><td>h₁</td><td>h₂</td><td>h₃</td><td>h₄</td><td>h₅</td><td>h₆</td></tr></tbody></table>
<div class="ts-formula">

$$p_i=\operatorname{softmax}(W_{\rm tag}h_i+b_{\rm tag}),\qquad
W_{\rm tag}\in\mathbb R^{K\times d}$$

</div>
<div class="ts-two"><div><strong>B / I / O</strong><p>Begin an entity, continue its type, or remain outside an entity.</p></div><div><strong>The same W and b at every position</strong><p>Different contextual states produce different distributions over K tags.</p></div></div>
<p class="ts-takeaway">“New York University” is one organization here—not three independent entities.</p>
<p class="s1-source">Authored annotation in a BIO convention; no model predictions shown. <a href="https://aclanthology.org/W03-0419/">CoNLL-2003: Tjong Kim Sang &amp; De Meulder (2003)</a>; <a href="https://aclanthology.org/N19-1423.pdf#page=9">BERT, §5.3</a>. Word-level states shown before subword alignment.</p>

::: {.notes}
TIME: 3 minutes. Contrast with one sentiment label for a review. NER labels entity
extent and type. PER denotes person, ORG organization, and O outside. Other task
labels such as location may exist; K is the size of the complete tag inventory,
not merely the tags occurring in this sentence. This is an authored BIO example,
not a claim about the exact serialization of a particular corpus release.
A shared head is applied at every selected word state. BERT still contextualizes
all positions. The tag at New begins an organization and York/University continue
it, even though New York alone could refer to a location in another context.
Independent token decisions can yield invalid BIO sequences; a CRF or constrained
decoding can add structure, but the BERT paper's §5.3 setup does not use a CRF.
Entity-level F1 requires correct span and type; token accuracy can hide boundary
errors. The next slide explains what a word state means when WordPiece splits it.
:::

## Word annotations must align with subword states {#ts-alignment .ts-slide}

<p class="ts-lead">Illustrative alignment: suppose “Lina” occupies two subword positions u₁, u₂.</p>
<table class="ts-align-table"><thead><tr><th>Encoder position</th><th>[CLS]</th><th>u₁</th><th>u₂</th><th>studies</th><th>…</th><th>[SEP]</th><th>[PAD]</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th>Original word</th><td>—</td><td colspan="2">Lina</td><td>studies</td><td>…</td><td>—</td><td>—</td></tr><tr><th>Scored target</th><td>ignore</td><td class="ts-person">B-PER</td><td>ignore</td><td>O</td><td>…</td><td>ignore</td><td>ignore</td></tr></tbody></table>
<div class="ts-formula">

$$\mathcal L_{\rm NER}=-\frac{1}{|I|}\sum_{i\in I}\log p_i(y_i),\qquad
I=\{\text{first subword of each labeled word}\}$$

</div>
<div class="ts-two"><div><strong>One annotation → one scored state</strong><p>Recover word boundaries using the tokenizer’s alignment metadata.</p></div><div><strong>Ignore a loss term ≠ remove context</strong><p>Continuation pieces remain encoder inputs and can affect scored states.</p></div></div>
<p class="ts-takeaway">Choose and document an alignment policy; duplicating labels changes the training objective.</p>
<p class="s1-source">First-subtoken policy follows <a href="https://aclanthology.org/N19-1423.pdf#page=9">Devlin et al. (2019), §5.3</a>. u₁/u₂ denote a hypothetical split, not an asserted tokenizer trace. Mean normalization is our explicit convention.</p>

::: {.notes}
TIME: 3 minutes. Start from word labels, then map them to subword positions. Never
zip labels with token IDs without checking alignment and special tokens. u1/u2 are
abstract pieces chosen to make a split visible; we do not report tokenization by
an installed model. The actual tokenizer supplies word IDs or character offsets.
The displayed policy scores only the first piece, as in BERT's NER setup. Another
policy may supervise all pieces with adjusted BIO continuation labels, but it changes
weighting and must be stated. Special tokens and padding have no tag loss here.
Ignore is a mask, not an extra label class. Continuation pieces still influence
context, so their paths can receive gradients through scored states during full
fine-tuning. Map predictions back to words before entity-span evaluation.
:::

## Extractive QA: condition on the question, locate the answer {#ts-qa .ts-slide}

<div class="s4-question"><b>QUESTION</b> Where does Lina study?<span><b>PASSAGE</b> Lina studies at <strong>New York University</strong>.</span></div>

{{< include assets/section4-diagrams/qa.html >}}

<p class="ts-takeaway">[CLS] question [SEP] passage [SEP] → question-conditioned passage states</p>
<p class="s1-source">Reuses the preserved QA diagram. Authored answerable example; displayed passage word indices 0–6. <a href="https://aclanthology.org/N19-1423.pdf#page=6">BERT, §4.2</a>. Real boundary labels use token positions and map back to source offsets.</p>

::: {.notes}
TIME: 3 minutes. Reuse the NER sentence but change the supervision: now a question
selects a contiguous span. Entity types alone cannot answer which span the question
asks about, and a QA answer need not be a named entity. The packed input lets the
passage states depend on the question. Only passage states are drawn, not the full
input sequence. Different questions can yield different contextual states for the
same passage. Two learned scoring vectors are shared across positions; they are not
per-position parameters. The diagram's edges are schematic dependencies, not learned
attention strengths or measured scores. Normalize over allowed passage positions.
This is answerable extraction as in SQuAD 1.1, not generation and not the QNLI
sentence-selection interface introduced in the encoder task overview.
:::

## Boundary supervision and constrained span decoding {#ts-span .ts-slide}

<p class="ts-source">Annotated answer: <strong>New York University</strong> · start a = 3, end b = 5 (word display)</p>
<div class="ts-formula ts-qa-math">

$$s_i=w_s^\top h_i,\quad e_i=w_e^\top h_i,\qquad
p_s(i)=\frac{e^{s_i}}{\sum_{k\in P}e^{s_k}},\quad
p_e(i)=\frac{e^{e_i}}{\sum_{k\in P}e^{e_k}}$$

$$\mathcal L_{\rm QA}=-\log p_s(a)-\log p_e(b)$$

</div>
<div class="ts-decode">

$$(\hat a,\hat b)=\underset{i,j\in P,\ i\le j,\ j-i+1\le L}{\operatorname{argmax}}\ (s_i+e_j)$$

<p>P: permitted passage positions · L: configured maximum answer length</p>
</div>
<p class="ts-takeaway">Independent maxima can give an invalid span. Decode a valid pair, then recover the passage substring.</p>
<p class="s1-source">Start/end model and ordered-span decoding: <a href="https://aclanthology.org/N19-1423.pdf#page=6">Devlin et al. (2019), §4.2</a>. Length bound is an explicit implementation constraint. No fabricated logits or numerical exercise.</p>

::: {.notes}
TIME: 4 minutes. Read s_i and e_i as scalar start/end logits at the same contextual
state h_i. Their softmax distributions are over positions, not the tag vocabulary
and not the language-model vocabulary. Gold boundaries derive from answer offsets;
our word-display indices must be remapped in a real subword tokenizer. All input
states can influence the boundary loss. A common implementation averages the two
negative log probabilities; our displayed sum differs only by a constant factor.
Maximizing s_i+e_j is equivalent to maximizing log p_s(i)+log p_e(j) for this fixed
input. The product of the two marginals is not normalized over only the valid spans.
L is a maximum number of token positions, not characters. Sliding windows and
truncated answers need explicit labeling policies for long passages. We do not
pretend that a truncated answer is present. For SQuAD 2.0, unanswerable questions
need a null-answer decision; BERT uses CLS as a null candidate and a tuned threshold.
That is a distinct setting, and its scores must not be mixed with SQuAD 1.1.
:::

## What does a SQuAD score measure? {#ts-metrics .ts-slide}

<p class="ts-source">Reference answer: <strong>New York University</strong> · a boundary error can retain partial overlap.</p>
<div class="ts-two ts-metric-cards"><div><span class="ts-label">EXACT MATCH · EM</span><strong>Complete answer agreement</strong><p>Does the normalized prediction match any reference answer?</p><p>Useful for detecting answer-boundary errors.</p></div><div><span class="ts-label">TOKEN-OVERLAP F1</span><strong>Partial lexical agreement</strong><p>Compute precision and recall from answer-token overlap; use the best reference.</p><p>Average question-level F1 across the dataset.</p></div></div>
<div class="ts-formula">

$$F_1=\frac{2PR}{P+R},\qquad
P=\frac{|A\cap G|}{|A|},\quad R=\frac{|A\cap G|}{|G|}$$

</div>
<p class="ts-takeaway">Neither metric proves reasoning quality. A high score still needs error analysis.</p>
<p class="s1-source"><a href="https://aclanthology.org/D16-1264.pdf#page=7">Rajpurkar et al. (2016), §6.1</a>. A/G are predicted/reference token multisets; intersection counts repeated tokens. Zero overlap yields F1 = 0. These are QA overlap metrics, not NER entity F1.</p>

::: {.notes}
TIME: 2 minutes. Define A as predicted answer tokens, G as a reference token multiset,
and P/R as precision/recall. Normalization precedes scoring. SQuAD evaluation
normalizes case, punctuation, articles, and whitespace. EM takes the best exact
match across references; F1 takes the best token-overlap F1 for each question and
then averages. This is not one global micro-F1 over all answer tokens. Explain the
qualitative effect of a prediction such as New York without turning this into an
arithmetic exercise: overlap remains but exact match fails against the full name.
Overlapping words do not establish semantic equivalence, and the benchmark does
not measure correctness of an external explanation. The next table reports both
metrics and keeps development and test splits separate.
:::

for example, the base/large single-model development columns. The enhanced test
rows must not be compared with development scores in the first two rows. The result
with 93.2 test F1 is a seven-system ensemble with prior TriviaQA adaptation. Do not
claim that 91.8 is the test result of the plain single model: that test number is
reported only for the extra-data condition. No error bars are available here.
:::
